title: U.S. cultural distance has widened on some political and consumer dimensions, but not everywhere
source_unit: Bertrand and Kamenica, NBER Working Paper 24771 and 2023 American Economic Journal: Applied Economics article
geography: United States; groups defined by income, education, gender, race, and political ideology; long-run cultural measures using multiple U.S. datasets

observations.period: 1965-2020-era measures as defined across the study's datasets; published 2023

denominator.unit: multi-dataset study of group distinguishability across media, consumer behavior, time use, attitudes, and newborn names

cultural_distance_definition.value: how accurately a person's group can be inferred from media consumption, consumer behavior, time use, social attitudes, or newborn name

political_ideology_and_attitudes.value: social-attitude differences by political ideology increased over the last four decades

income_and_attitudes.value: social-attitude differences by income increased somewhat over the last four decades

race_and_consumer_behavior.value: Whites and non-Whites converged somewhat on attitudes but diverged in consumer behavior

other_dimensions.value: many other group-by-dimension combinations remained broadly constant; gender time-use differences narrowed through 1995 and then stabilized

observations.method: Long-run comparison of cultural-distance measures across U.S. datasets, using group classification from media diet, consumer behavior, time use, social attitudes, and newborn names; the record preserves study-level patterns rather than treating all measures as one scale.
observations.uncertainty: The datasets, group definitions, periods, and measures differ. Classification accuracy is not the same as hostility, social isolation, partisan sorting, causal polarization, or unequal welfare. A stable average distance can hide subgroup change, and a widening distance does not identify its cause.
observations.subgroup: Income, education, gender, race, and political-ideology groups across the study's separate cultural dimensions and time periods.
observations.counterinterpretation: Greater distinguishability may reflect real group-specific preferences, market segmentation, data availability, or improved measurement rather than social conflict. Convergence on attitudes can coexist with divergence in consumption, and political-cultural distance does not imply that people never interact or cooperate.

related_sources.claim: Published American Economic Journal: Applied Economics version, volume 15(4), pages 100-141, 2023.

boundary: This finding measures cultural distance as group distinguishability across several U.S. cultural dimensions. It does not measure polarization as a whole, explain why distance changed, show reduced contact or trust, or establish that cultural distance produced political action, exclusion, or policy change.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: NBER abstract and published AEA metadata reviewed for definition, group dimensions, periods, and headline patterns; underlying multi-dataset estimates are not re-pooled here.
